blocking.issue: checkLogout/isClearingSetCookie can pass F9 while logout is broken. It runs its regexes over res.headers.get('set-cookie'), which Node joins with ', ', and it matches the cookie name with a substring includes('growmax-admin='). It never checks the growmax-admin cookie's own Max-Age/Expires or its Path, and on a pass it just sets A.cookie = null, so the isAdmin:false follow-up holds against any server. Against a local 127.0.0.1 mock (the session returns isAdmin:true whenever the admin cookie is still valid), F9 PASSED for all three of these broken logouts: (1) Set-Cookie 'other=; Max-Age=0' followed by 'growmax-admin=<sealed>; Max-Age=86400' (admin session re-set, still admin); (2) 'growmax-admin=; Path=/api/admin; Max-Age=0' (a browser keeps the Path=/ login cookie, so the user stays logged in); (3) only 'xgrowmax-admin=; Max-Age=0'. The task requires that 'an app regression that stops clearing the cookie must still fail F9'.
blocking.fix: Use res.headers.getSetCookie(). Select the entry whose name before '=' is exactly 'growmax-admin'. Require that entry's own attributes to clear the cookie (Max-Age<=0, or a parsed Expires in the past). Require its Path, and its Domain if either side sets one, to equal the login cookie's, which F4 captured. Only then drop that cookie from the jar and do the session GET. Add mock cases for the three scenarios above to functional/selftest-p5.3.mjs.

blocking.issue:
F9 still passes broken logouts, because checkLogout and isClearingCookieAttrs read cookie attributes differently from RFC 6265 and from browsers. The mock (/tmp/rev2/exp/f9mock.mjs, 127.0.0.1) returns isAdmin:true whenever the sealed admin cookie is still sent, and its login sets growmax-admin=<sealed> with Path=/ and Max-Age=86400. F9 reported PASS for four broken cases:
(a) The logout sends 'growmax-admin=; Max-Age=0' with no Path attribute. pathMatches treats a missing Path as '/'. A browser instead uses the default-path of POST /api/admin/logout, which is /api/admin (RFC 6265 §5.1.4). That clear misses the Path=/ login cookie, so the user stays admin. This is the same wrong-Path class as round 1, reached by leaving the attribute out.
(b) The logout sends 'growmax-admin=<sealed>; Path=/; Max-Age=86400; Expires=<1970>'. A valid Max-Age takes precedence over Expires (§5.3 step 3), so the cookie is kept for 24h. The code counts the past Expires as a clear.
(c) The logout sends 'Max-Age=' (empty or whitespace). Number('') is 0, so the code counts it as a clear. Browsers ignore an invalid Max-Age and keep the cookie.
(d) A.loginCookieAttrs is null, which happens whenever F4 did not capture an exact-name growmax-admin entry. The code then skips the Path/Domain check (`!loginAttrs ||`), so a clear on Path=/api/admin passes.
In each case the harness sets A.cookie = null by itself, so the follow-up isAdmin:false says nothing about what a browser would still send.
blocking.fix:
1. Parse Max-Age only if it matches /^-?\d+$/ after trimming. If a valid Max-Age is present, it alone decides (<=0 clears), and Expires is ignored. Otherwise use a parsed Expires in the past.
2. Compute each cookie's effective Path as RFC 6265 does: use the attribute if it starts with '/'; otherwise use the default-path of the request that set the cookie (for /api/admin/login and /api/admin/logout both, that is /api/admin). Compare logout's effective Path with login's.
3. Fail closed when loginCookieAttrs is null: F9 fails with a detail saying no login cookie attributes were captured.
4. Add mock cases (a)-(d) to functional/selftest-p5.3.mjs, driving captureSetCookie on a mock login response rather than setting LOGIN_COOKIE_ATTRS by hand.
The real app still passes after this fix: iron-session 8.0.4's destroy() sets maxAge:0, and Next's cookie normalizer adds Path=/, so logout emits Path=/ and Max-Age=0.

blocking.issue:
F9 can still pass a broken logout. `parseCookieAttrs` (run.mjs:69-91) doesn't follow RFC 6265 §5.2 in two places. I ran each case against a 127.0.0.1 mock (`/tmp/rev3/exp/f9.mjs`) through the real `requestJson`, `captureSetCookie` and `checkLogout`. The login sets `growmax-admin=<sealed>; Path=/; Max-Age=86400`, and the mock's session route returns isAdmin:true whenever the sealed cookie is sent. F9 reported PASS for all of these:
(1) Logout sends `growmax-admin; Path=/; Max-Age=0`, with no '=' in the name-value pair. §5.2 step 2 says to ignore such a set-cookie-string entirely; RFC 6265bis and Chrome instead store it as a cookie with an empty name. Either way the sealed growmax-admin cookie is kept. The parser reads it as name 'growmax-admin' with an empty value, so it counts as a clear.
(2) Logout re-sends the sealed value with an Expires that V8's lenient `Date.parse` accepts but the RFC 6265 §5.1.1 cookie-date algorithm rejects: `Expires=0` (parsed as 2000-01-01), `Expires=2020` or `Expires=-1`. Browsers ignore that Expires, so the sealed cookie becomes a session cookie and the user stays admin. The harness counts the past date as a clear.
In every case `clearsAdminCookie` becomes true and run.mjs:577 sets `A.cookie = null`. The follow-up GET then reports isAdmin:false no matter what a browser would still send. The task requires that an app regression that stops clearing the cookie must still fail F9.
blocking.fix:
1. In `parseCookieAttrs`, when the name-value pair has no '=' or the trimmed name is empty, return a name that never matches (for example null), so the entry is never selected as the admin cookie.
2. Parse Expires with the RFC 6265 §5.1.1 cookie-date algorithm: day-of-month, month, year and hh:mm:ss are all required, plus the year fix-ups. The minimum is to accept only the IMF-fixdate form, `^[A-Za-z]{3}, \d{2} [A-Za-z]{3} \d{4} \d{2}:\d{2}:\d{2} GMT$`. Treat anything else as no Expires.
3. Defence in depth: for the follow-up GET, don't set `A.cookie = null`. Put `growmax-admin=<value from the logout entry>` in the jar instead, which is what the browser would hold if the harness misread the expiry. The real app's clear has an empty value, and `/api/admin/session` reads that as not admin, so the real app still passes. A regression that re-sends the sealed value then fails, even if some other expiry syntax is misread.
4. Add these cases to `functional/selftest-p5.3.mjs`: no '=' in the name-value pair; sealed value with `Expires=0`, `Expires=2020` and `Expires=-1`. Also keep a case for a correct Expires-only clear with a valid IMF date.

nonBlocking: F9: a clear that carries `Partitioned` (CHIPS) is accepted as clearing an unpartitioned login cookie. Chrome stores partitioned cookies under their own key, so the login cookie would survive. This is an unlikely regression. A simple guard is to require that the Partitioned flag matches between login and logout.
F9 `Expires` also accepts forms that browsers do parse but RFC 6265 does not strictly require. The IMF-fixdate restriction in the blocking fix covers this.

Parity, already known: the hashed-prefix normalization (`HASHED_ASSET_PREFIX_RE` = `/^\/_next\/static\/[^/]+\//`) collapses the first segment under `/_next/static/`, including `chunks`. So a ref renamed from `/_next/static/chunks/X` to `/_next/static/chunkz/X` compares equal. This comes from HEAD, not from this change. hashedCssSha256 covers CSS content; JS directory moves are not checked.

Parity, already known and allowed by the spec: an http downgrade, an added #fragment, or www vs bare growmax.io on a canonical link all compare equal after `reclassifyLinks`. Only path+search is compared.

Parity, already known and allowed by the spec: an absolute link from B to its own vercel.app host is treated as same-site. That would hide a leaked NEXT_PUBLIC_SITE_URL=vercel.app in body links before cutover. Before cutover, grep B's HTML for vercel.app hrefs.

F2: any hand-written or backfilled marker that lacks an integer `countBefore` counts as the cap. That includes a marker in the task's minimal format of runLabel, sentAt and base. It fails closed, but it blocks F2 until someone removes it. Document this for the orchestrator.
F2 markers live in this container only. A verifier in another container relies on STATE flags.demoTestsSent alone, which reads 2. This is organizational, as noted before.
